transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2025-01-10 | Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: 42m | Location: Zoom
Attendees: Emma Li (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Maria Gomez (CTO, Cinder Labs), Alan Cho (Backend), Priya Nair (ML)

Summary: Quick hosted API demo focused on streaming/chat basics, parameter tradeoffs, and Redwood 'Livetrace' per-request trace UI. Went through retry/rescue patterns (canary fallback to smaller model), console traces, and Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization. Customer concerns: latency targets for interactive agents (~200-300ms per token), data residency, and cost.

Topics covered: Livetrace (new trace UI), streaming behavior, temperature/top-p tuning, max_tokens and truncation, prefix/KV cache mentions, retry strategy (exponential backoff, idempotency), console usage for traces and per-route cost, Optimize suggestions.

[00:00] Emma (Redwood): Hey all, quick intros, I'm Emma in AE, and Ravi is our SE. Thanks for carving time. Maria: want to kick off with your main goals?
[00:18] Maria (Cinder): Yeah thanks. We're building a realtime assistant inside our dashboard; need low-latency responses and predictable cost. Main devs are on this call - Alan and Priya. Looking for hosted option first, maybe private later.
[00:34] Ravi (Redwood SE): Great, we'll do a short live demo of the hosted API streaming path, show the console "Livetrace" — that's our per-request trace — and then walk through retry and fallback patterns.
[00:46] Alan: Quick question, when you say streaming, is it chunked SSE style or web sockets? We have a websocket layer today.
[00:54] Ravi: We support chunked streaming over HTTP/2 and SSE, websockets are supported in SDK helpers. For your websocket gateway you can pipe chunks through — there might be slight reordering if you buffer locally, but usually fine.
[01:12] Priya: What's the per-token latency on the hosted models? Our SLA target is ~200-300ms/token at 1-2 concurrent users per session.
[01:22] Emma: Short answer: depends on model and seq length. We'll demo LiveTrace to show p99 and per-kv-cache hits. For many of our optimized open models you can hit ~120-250ms/token for short prefixes on gpus. For production we can propose a dedicated pool.
[01:40] Ravi: (screen share) Opening the console — Livetrace view. You can see token-by-token timings, kernel selection, and batch windows. Note the red/amber markers — those indicate fallback events or cold KV cash misses.
[02:02] Speaker 2: There's a small glitch in the transcription, but you can see the trace shows batching at 8ms windows.
[02:12] Emma: Important config bits: keep response streaming enabled for UX, but cap max_tokens to avoid runaway costs. Use temperature 0.0-0.6 for deterministic replies; top_p is helpful for creative flows.
[02:30] Maria: We have a mix of short system prompts and long context docs. How should we set context window and truncation?
[02:38] Ravi: Two patterns: pre-encode docs into embeddings and fetch relevant context per turn (reduces token cost), or use a rolling window with trimmed history. The console shows memory pressure when the model KV grows. For long docs optimize with chunking + RAG.
[02:58] Alan: On retries: if the stream drops mid-response what's the recommended client behavior? Re-request full response or partial resume?
[03:06] Ravi: Best practice: make your calls idempotent with an idempotency_key; on mid-stream failure re-call using the same key and a 'resume' param if you store last token index. Many teams re-generate from last confirmed turn. We recommend exponential backoff 100ms * 2^n with jitter.
[03:38] Priya: Can Redwood do automatic model fallback? e.g., if the gpt-large instance is busy, drop to a quantized variant?
[03:45] Emma: Yes, smart routing can fallback to compatible variant (we call them 'model families'). You can configure fallbacks per route in the Console and set SLOs.
[03:58] Maria: Is there a cost tradeoff panel? We need to estimate cost per session.
[04:04] Ravi: Console has per-route token cost breakdown and Optimize will suggest batching windows and quantization settings. We demo a sample workload and it suggests batching window of 16ms and int8 quant for the tail calls.
[04:26] Emma: Quick demo: make a streaming call from the sandbox. (typing) Using our sandbox key, I'll call /v1/chat/stream with messages array, stream=true, temp=0.2, max_tokens=150.
[04:44] [04:44] API: -> stream chunks begin
[04:46] Ravi: Notice first chunk comes in 60ms, then steady at ~120ms per token. Livetrace shows a KV miss at token 10 — you can see cache warmup.
[05:10] Priya: That KV miss: can we prewarm or pin prefixes?
[05:15] Ravi: Yes, prefix caching and pinned warmers in Dedicated help. For hosted we recommend a warmup call at session start. We also expose a cache hit metric in the trace so you can set alerts.
[05:34] Alan: How do we handle long-running ephemeral conversations where tokens accumulate? We worry about latency spikes.
[05:42] Ravi: Trim history, summarize older turns server-side, and use embeddings for doc context. Also use shorter max_tokens and rely on the agent to call external tools for long ops. Console shows historical latency correlated with seq length.
[06:05] Maria: Security — we need SOC2, SSO, and VPC peering options for production. Also KMS for key management.
[06:15] Emma: We're SOC2 Type II, SSO via SAML, and Private deployments support customer-managed VPC with KMS/HSM integrations. We'll send the stack doc and our network diagram.
[06:30] Maria: Great. Also curious about throttling and rate limiting — we have bursty traffic.
[06:36] Ravi: You can set per-account quotas and per-route throttles. For spikes we recommend burst capacity or a dedicated pool. There are graceful fallback policies that will return degraded responses from a smaller model instead of full failures.
[07:02] Emma: Back to retries — important to mark idempotency, log request ids, and have the client perform partial reconnection logic. We'll share a client-side snippet.
[07:12] Speaker 3: (unintelligible)
[07:16] Priya: For perf benching, can we run JMeter or locust against the hosted sandbox or do you prefer dedicated?
[07:22] Ravi: For realistic GPU perf use Dedicated or a perf bench we run in coordination. Sandbox is fine for functional tests but not perf at scale. We'll set up a perf run on a mirror environment.
[07:40] Emma: Demo of Optimize suggestions in Console: it surfaced a 18% token cost reduction by enabling prefix caching and reducing batch window from 20ms to 12ms for this workload. Also shows expected quality delta when suggesting int8 quant.
[08:00] Maria: Quality regressions are a concern. How do we monitor?
[08:06] Ravi: We have quality monitoring tied to evals — you can upload prompts and golden outputs; Console will webhook on regressions and show drift. We can also run A/B traffic splits for rollouts.
[08:28] Alan: Anything about idempotency for tool calls? For our integrations we call external ticketing systems.
[08:34] Ravi: Tool-calling should be transactional on your side; we recommend dedupe ids and server-side writes be idempotent. Redwood can attach request metadata to help tracing.
[08:50] Emma: Quick walk through of sample retry pseudo-code and client snippet for resumable stream. (pastes snippet) Note: use request_id and last_event_index.
[09:10] [09:10] (small audio drop)
[09:16] Priya: You mentioned batch sizing earlier — what's a safe starting point?
[09:22] Ravi: Start with 8--16 tokens batching for interactive use, ramp to 32 for high throughput. Use Optimize to recommend based on your latency SLOs.
[09:38] Maria: Who owns the billing for Dedicated? If we move there mid-poc.
[09:44] Emma: Dedicated is reserved capacity contracts, we can start with hosted usage and then migrate; billing will be contract-based for Dedicated and usage/seat for hosted. We'll provide a sample cost comparison.
[10:02] Alan: Any note about region residency? Our EU customers need data in EU.
[10:08] Emma: We have region pins for hosted and Private/VPC options. We'll include regions supported and data residency notes in the security packet.
[10:22] Maria: Let's talk about a concrete rescue plan: if model A fails, fallback to model B, and if that fails return cached summary.
[10:30] Ravi: Exactly — config: primary model -> secondary quant variant -> cached synthesized response -> 503 with degraded toaster. Console shows route-level fallback chain and metrics.
[10:48] Priya: Can we simulate failover during benching?
[10:52] Ravi: Yes, we can inject faults in a perf run to test fallback. We'll coordinate that in the perf plan.
[11:04] Emma: Quick Q&A — Maria asked about latency budgeting per token vs end-to-end. We recommend token-level SLOs in Console plus synthetic checks.
[11:18] Maria: Ok this is helpful. Next steps?
[11:22] Emma: We'll send the sandbox, quickstart notebook, SOC2 + network diagram, and propose perf run times. Ravi will own perf plan.
[11:30] Alan: I'll share our top user flows and a few sample prompts.
[11:36] Priya: Also send the sample JMeter script if possible.
[11:40] Emma: Yep. Any final concerns?
[11:44] Maria: Nothing major, just want clear SLAs and a way to measure regressions.
[11:50] Ravi: We'll attach the eval flow and show how to set alerting.
[12:02] Closing summary: next steps and action items repeated.

Recap (as spoken):
- Demo covered hosted streaming path, Livetrace UI, retry/resume patterns, and Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization.
- Security: send SOC2, SAML/SSO details, VPC options.
- Perf: schedule bench involving Ravi and Priya; customer to provide flows.

End of transcript.
